brief.head: Genes for hockey?
brief.text: Nature and nur­ture are cor­re­lated, Ajay Shah said. A hockey fam­ily passes on genes for ex­plo­sive strength and early coach­ing, so we over­state what na­ture alone hands down. {125-C06}

brief.head: Newton’s way out
brief.text: Newton rec­on­ciled sci­ence and faith, Ajay Shah said: God made laws like grav­ity, set the sys­tem going and let it whirl along. Biology al­lows the same move. {125-S03}

lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on the forces that made us
lead.head: Know thyself, meet thy genes

pic.caption: Ajay Shah (left) and Amit Varma early in Episode 125

body: Know thy­self, urged the philoso­phers[[x1]] of an­cient Greece. One way to do it, Amit Varma said, is to un­der­stand your hard­wiring: the way evo­lu­tion shaped you, and the sep­a­rate way cul­ture shaped you. {#knowthyself}

Ajay Shah’s turn­ing point came as an eco­nom­ics PhD stu­dent, when he read Paul Ewald’s ar­ti­cle on the evo­lu­tion of vir­u­lence in *Scientific American*. “It just blew my mind and it was just a mo­ment that you can’t unsee,” he said. {125-S02}

Varma came to it later, through Steven Pinker’s *The Blank Slate*: the sec­ond great in­tel­lec­tual awak­en­ing of his life, after mar­kets. Both, he said, share a bot­tom-up process of spon­ta­neous order, with “no cen­tral plan­ner, no grand de­signer”[[x2]]. {125-S01}
## Six state­ments
Before the bi­ol­ogy, Varma cleared away mis­con­cep­tions with five state­ments, then added a sixth.

The first was that nat­u­ral se­lec­tion is in­de­pen­dent of God. William Paley saw in a watch on a beach, and in the human eye, the hand of a de­signer. “Darwin made the ex­is­tence of a metaphor­i­cal watch­maker ir­rel­e­vant,” Varma said. {125-C03}
Nor does na­ture set­tle what is good. Deriving an ought from an is, or equat­ing the nat­u­ral with the good, is a fal­lacy, Varma ar­gued, on the right and the left alike.
Nature and nur­ture are not a bi­nary ei­ther. In a line Varma at­tributes to Steven Pinker, na­ture gives you knobs, and nur­ture turns them. {125-C05}
His last warn­ings were about lan­guage and pur­pose. Genes want noth­ing, and evo­lu­tion aims at noth­ing. “There is no mother evo­lu­tion,” Shah said.
## Copies and com­pe­ti­tion

The mech­a­nism it­self is bare, Shah said: things that copy them­selves, vari­a­tion among them, and fi­nite re­sources to fight over. The traits that win are re­fined, gen­er­a­tion after gen­er­a­tion, with no apex and no end­point. {125-C10}

Sex shuf­fles genes and mul­ti­plies the vari­a­tion se­lec­tion works on, and mate choice adds a sec­ond en­gine. The two can clash: the springbok’s high leap im­presses mates, but the lion sim­ply waits for it to land. {125-C11}

Environment acts through gene ex­pres­sion. Children starved in the womb dur­ing the 1944 famine in Amsterdam grew up more prone to obe­sity, Shah said. Their DNA was un­changed, Varma stressed, so this was epi­ge­net­ics, not Lamarckism. {125-C12}
Then came the ex­am­ples, which Shah called wild: sickle cell and malaria, milk-drinking adults, Korea’s div­ing women, Britain’s black­ened moths and cholera in the two Bengals.
## In no hurry
The unit of evo­lu­tion­ary time, Shah said, is the gen­er­a­tion. {125-C14} Humans man­age one every 25 years, about 400 in 10,000 years, so we are mostly the hu­mans of 10,000 years ago.
Modernity, on that clock, has barely begun. “It was only the day be­fore yes­ter­day that the Magna Carta hap­pened,” he said. {125-J19}

Varma’s final point was that the brain is part of the body, shaped by se­lec­tion like every other organ, so some dif­fer­ences be­tween men and women are hard­wired. Admitting that, he in­sisted, does not jus­tify treat­ing any­one un­equally. {125-C15}
That ar­gu­ment con­tin­ues in a sec­ond part, built around Ogi Ogas and Sai Gaddam’s *A Billion Wicked Thoughts*, which Varma calls a mas­ter­piece.

Shah closed with a moral. Marvel at the eagle’s eye and re­sist the engineer’s urge to de­sign one, he said: “this magic is made by an un­con­trolled self-organizing sys­tem with­out any de­signer.” {125-C01}
Varma had the last word: “The only kind of eye I don’t like, Ajay, is the I in ego.” {125-J13}

second.label: Malaria’s bargain
second.head: The lion or the mosquito
second.deck: Ajay Shah on why a disorder that fells runners has survived

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on sickle cell and malaria

body: Sickle cell anaemia looks like a cruel flaw. Push the heart hard, Ajay Shah said, and red blood cells col­lapse into a sickle shape, so a per­son run­ning from a leop­ard can crash to the ground. Why had such a trait not died out?

The an­swer is malaria. {125-S07} Its plas­mod­ium hides in­side red blood cells, out of reach of the im­mune sys­tem, and mul­ti­plies there. {#plasmodium} A sick­led cell makes its life much harder.

Evolution struck a bal­ance be­tween peak car­diac ca­pa­bil­ity and sur­viv­ing malaria, Shah said, which is why en­tire com­mu­ni­ties in India carry sickle cell and tha­las­saemia. Amit Varma pro­posed a title for the short story: “The Lion and the Mosquito.” Shah cor­rected him: “The Lion or the Mosquito.” {125-J08}

quote.text: It turns out that tha­lassemia and sickle cell ane­mia are se­lected for in en­vi­ron­ments with malaria.

third.head: Black is the new white

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on the moths of industrial England

body: British moths were once white or off-white, Ajay Shah said. Then the in­dus­trial rev­o­lu­tion brought poor-quality coal fur­naces, their soot set­tled on build­ings, and the walls turned black.

A white moth on a black wall was easy prey for birds. Darker moths sur­vived bet­ter, and “within a cou­ple of decades the moths of in­dus­trial rev­o­lu­tion England turned black.” The ex­am­ple played a big role in the ear­li­est de­bates over evo­lu­tion. {125-S10}
Amit Varma spelt out the mech­a­nism. Every gen­er­a­tion throws up a few ran­dom dark mu­tants, and the en­vi­ron­ment de­cides which sur­vive. {#mutants}

The same process, he said, breeds mos­qui­toes that re­sist in­sec­ti­cides and bac­te­ria that re­sist an­tibi­otics. Even if only 0.5 per cent of mos­qui­toes re­sist a treat­ment, those are the ones that sur­vive and breed. {#halfpercent}

p2.title: How we were made
p2.deck: From God and the watchmaker to the brain, Amit Varma and Ajay Shah lay out natural selection

quote.text: God made the laws. And He got a sys­tem going, and then the sys­tem whirled along.

box.title: Darwin’s new cosmology
box.text: Ghiselin, quoted by Amit Varma, said peo­ple could not han­dle the rad­i­cal de­par­ture im­plicit in Darwin’s new cos­mol­ogy: “A world in which the brain is it­self an ex­ten­sion of the go­nads sim­ply can­not be rec­on­ciled with the old way of think­ing.” {125-J15}

sections.label: Starting points
sections.head: Watch, but no watchmaker
sections.caption: God, Paley and the watchmaker
body: Before any bi­ol­ogy, Amit Varma set out state­ments to clear away mis­con­cep­tions. The first: nat­u­ral se­lec­tion is in­de­pen­dent of God and of moral­ity.

William Paley ar­gued that a watch[[x7]] found on a beach, un­like a stone, must have a maker, and that the in­tri­cate human eye must like­wise have a de­signer: God. Natural se­lec­tion showed that ran­dom ac­ci­dents of na­ture could build such in­tri­cacy from the bot­tom up. {125-C03}
That does not rule God out, Varma said. A be­liever can say God is so cool that he cre­ated the process called nat­u­ral se­lec­tion.

Ajay Shah of­fered Newton’s rec­on­cil­i­a­tion: God made the laws, set the sys­tem going and let it whirl along. Biology al­lows the same move, he said, plac­ing God at the first self-replicating mol­e­cules, or at the Big Bang. {125-S03}
## Is does not make ought

The sec­ond state­ment warned against David Hume’s is-ought fal­lacy[[x6]], which de­rives a pre­scrip­tion from a de­scrip­tion, and G. E. Moore’s nat­u­ral­is­tic fal­lacy, which de­fines the good as the nat­u­ral. {#hume}

Bigots once called ho­mo­sex­u­al­ity un­nat­u­ral and so wrong, Varma said: a fal­lacy, and false be­sides. He faults Jordan Peterson on gen­der roles, and the left for deny­ing dif­fer­ences be­tween the sexes.

~ With what Adam Smith called the man of sys­tem, these fal­la­cies fed early-20th-century eu­gen­ics on the left as well as the right, Varma said: H. G. Wells and George Bernard Shaw be­lieved in it too. {125-J16}

quote.text: God made the laws. And He got a sys­tem going, and then the sys­tem whirled along.

sections.label: Nature and nurture
sections.head: Wired one way, raised another
sections.caption: nature’s knobs
body: Nature and nur­ture are not a bi­nary, Amit Varma said. He likes a line he is “pretty sure”[[x9]][[x8]] is Steven Pinker’s, though nei­ther he nor AI has found its source. {125-C05}

We are hard­wired dif­fer­ently, he ex­plained. Someone pre­dis­posed to anger can stay calm in a peace­ful life. A placid per­son can lose his cool in a nasty, brutish one, or, Varma of­fered, if he keeps meet­ing Bengali econ­o­mists. {125-J03}
Culture’s role, he ar­gued, is to mit­i­gate or am­plify that hard­ware ac­cord­ing to val­ues we ar­rive at by think­ing. That, to him, is the whole Enlightenment project.
## Old wiring, new world

Ajay Shah listed the old wiring: a crav­ing for fat and sugar from times of scarce food, a hair-trigger fight-or-flight re­sponse, and trib­al­ism from bands with a me­dian size of 150 peo­ple. {#tribe} Culture is the op­er­at­ing sys­tem on top.
Shah also warned that we over­state na­ture. Talent seems to run in fam­i­lies partly be­cause fam­i­lies pass on coach­ing and en­cour­age­ment along with genes. {125-C06}

~ Varma added that so­cial media com­pa­nies chas­ing en­gage­ment have ac­ci­den­tally am­pli­fied our tribal in­stincts. As the rain poured down, he said, it was up to us to re­mem­ber that the rain too will stop.

quote.text: Nature gives you knobs, nur­ture turns them.

sections.label: The mechanics
sections.head: Copy, vary, compete, repeat
sections.caption: the bare mechanics of selection
body: Natural se­lec­tion needs lit­tle, Ajay Shah said. There must be things that make copies of them­selves, or­gan­isms or even firms. {#copies} Their traits must vary. And re­sources must be fi­nite, so they com­pete.

Better users of re­sources leave more copies, so their traits spread and, gen­er­a­tion after gen­er­a­tion, are re­fined “to fiendish lev­els of ex­cel­lence”. There is no equal­ity in it, and no end.

Amit Varma il­lus­trated it with taste. Among fruit and poi­sonous plants, a mu­ta­tion for lik­ing bit­ter things could kill its car­rier, so the sweet tooth and the aver­sion to bit­ter­ness spread. {#bitter}

Culture shapes taste too, within lim­its. He read out Ogi Ogas and Sai Gaddam: “We can learn to ap­pre­ci­ate food that is bit­ter, like cof­fee or olives, but no cul­ture en­joys cin­na­mon sprin­kled feces.” {125-J18}
## The sec­ond en­gine

Sex, some three bil­lion years ago, was an in­cred­i­ble in­no­va­tion, Shah said: it shuf­fles genes and mul­ti­plies vari­a­tion. {#threebillion} In com­plex crea­tures, mate choice adds a sec­ond en­gine, sex­ual se­lec­tion.
~ The en­gines can pull apart. A spring­bok leaps high when chased, sig­nalling health to mates, while the lion waits for it to land. Varma called it “a race to the top”. {125-J06}

quote.text: Evolution never ends. There is no apex out­come, there is no des­ti­na­tion.

sections.label: Epigenetics
sections.head: The famine’s long shadow
sections.caption: the Amsterdam famine
body: If every human cell holds fixed DNA, two bil­lion let­ters of it at birth, Ajay Shah asked, is ev­ery­thing about us pro­grammed? {#twobillion}
No. Epigenetics, he said, stud­ies gene ex­pres­sion: the way the en­vi­ron­ment in­ter­acts with the code writ­ten in DNA to pro­duce dif­fer­ent out­comes.
One of its most fa­mous stud­ies con­cerns Amsterdam in 1944. After a re­bel­lion, the Nazis cut off the roads to starve the city. The Allies air­dropped food, but a ter­ri­ble famine fol­lowed.

Years later, sci­en­tists stud­ied chil­dren ex­posed to the famine be­tween con­cep­tion and birth. Those starved in the womb had a much greater propen­sity to obe­sity, hoard­ing food more des­per­ately, and the ef­fect lasted sev­eral gen­er­a­tions. {125-S13}
## Not Lamarck’s way

That sounds weirdly Lamarckian, Shah con­ceded. Amit Varma drew the line. Lamarckism holds that changes made in your life­time, like a blacksmith’s strong arms, pass on through your genes. It was a com­mon be­lief in the 19th cen­tury, and there is noth­ing to it. {125-S04}
~ The famine changed no one’s DNA, Varma said. It turned the sweet­ness knob up full, and the chil­dren ended up eat­ing “a lot of lad­doos, if lad­doos were ever in Amsterdam”. {125-J07}

quote.text: Epigenetics did not change the DNA of the kids who were born at that time. It merely turned the knobs dif­fer­ently.

sections.label: Deep time
sections.head: The clock ticks in generations
sections.caption: evolution’s slow clock
body: Hearing that moths turned black in a few decades, peo­ple make a com­mon mis­take, Ajay Shah warned: the com­pres­sion of time. {#compression}

Large mu­ta­tions are gen­er­ally a mis­take, he said. Big changes are birth de­fects. Picture, he said, a com­plete mos­quito with one tiny change: a lit­tle more abil­ity to cope with DDT. The ma­chine being mod­i­fied is so com­pli­cated that too many changes at once make a mess. What works is a tiny change, ac­cu­mu­lated over hun­dreds or thou­sands of gen­er­a­tions.
That is how the eye was pol­ished, in­clud­ing the eagle’s, which from two kilo­me­tres up can see a sin­gle mouse walk­ing on the ground. {#eagle}
## Ten min­utes or 25 years

Bacteria re­pro­duce roughly every ten min­utes, six gen­er­a­tions an hour: a fright­en­ing pace that has made cop­ing with them a major evo­lu­tion­ary force, shap­ing the human im­mune sys­tem. {#tenminutes}

Humans man­age one gen­er­a­tion every 25 years[[x10]], Shah said: 400 in 10,000 years, which isn’t much. {#fourhundred} So we are mostly the hu­mans of 10,000 years ago, and our hard­ware has not evolved for mod­ern con­di­tions.
~ Peace, civil­i­sa­tion and the rule of law are, by that mea­sure, brand new. “The Magna Carta is 1215,” Shah said, “it’s like blink of an eye.” {125-J19}

quote.text: The unit of evo­lu­tion­ary timescale is not time, but gen­er­a­tions

art.caption: Ajay Shah on evolution’s slow clock

sections.label: The brain
sections.head: It doesn’t stop at the neck
sections.caption: the brain as part of the body
body: Amit Varma ended with a point he called al­most ob­vi­ous. Every cell of the body is de­signed by nat­u­ral se­lec­tion, so why imag­ine the brain is not? {125-C15}
No one de­nies that male and fe­male bod­ies evolved dif­fer­ently, he said. Yet when it comes to the brain and be­hav­iour, many peo­ple talk as if ev­ery­thing is cul­ture.

Varma did not wave cul­ture away. Society is pa­tri­ar­chal, he said, and cul­tures mag­nify some of the worst as­pects of our na­ture. But many dif­fer­ences be­tween men and women are also hard­wired[[x11]].
## Aware, not un­equal
The task, he ar­gued, is to be aware of those dif­fer­ences rather than deny them, and not to con­clude that they re­quire un­equal treat­ment.

Ajay Shah had ear­lier made a re­lated point: the voice in our heads is one evo­lu­tion­ary adap­ta­tion among many, and much of what drives us runs below aware­ness. There is com­pli­cated cir­cuitry, he noted, that makes the heart beat. {#heartbeat}

~ The episode was ground­work. The hosts had meant to fold it into their episode on Ogi Ogas and Sai Gaddam’s *A Billion Wicked Thoughts*, but split it in two, lest that be­come, in Varma’s words, “like a *Seen and the Unseen* eight-hour episode”. {125-J12}

quote.text: The brain is a part of the body, right? Every cell of our body is de­signed, as you pointed out, by nat­u­ral se­lec­tion, right?

Evolution is the ul­ti­mate suc­cess story of spon­ta­neous order. That there is no cen­tral plan­ner, there is no tele­ol­ogy, there is no ob­jec­tive, the sys­tem just keeps evolv­ing on its own, and my God, it does amaz­ing things.

p3.title: Selected stories
p3.deck: Diving women, milk drinkers and superbugs: evolution at work, and what it teaches

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on how clean water tamed a killer
stories.head: A tale of two Bengals
body: In the early years after in­de­pen­dence, Ajay Shah said, West Bengal im­proved its drink­ing water and cut its fae­cal con­tam­i­na­tion. In East Bengal, things stayed bad.

What fol­lowed was evo­lu­tion at work. Where dirty water all but guar­an­teed that cholera reached new vic­tims, it had no rea­son to keep its host alive. It killed fast, forc­ing the host into “crazy di­ar­rhea” that in­fected the water sup­ply.

In West Bengal, where trans­mis­sion got harder, “the in­cen­tives of the cholera changed”[[x12]], Shah said, cred­it­ing “the glo­ries of the Republic of India”. Its strains evolved to be less vir­u­lent. {125-S12}

The idea comes from Paul Ewald, whose *Scientific American* ar­ti­cle on the evo­lu­tion of vir­u­lence hooked Shah on bi­ol­ogy. A pathogen uses its host’s body to copy it­self, then must jump to an­other host. Kill the host within a day or two, and it can­not get its copies out.

So a pathogen that passes fee­bly does best by keep­ing its host alive, while one that spreads eas­ily can be ra­pa­cious. Depending on the com­plex­ity of trans­mis­sion, Shah said, there is an op­ti­mal level of vir­u­lence. {125-C13}

He ap­plied the logic to Covid. In a crowded Bombay sub­ur­ban train or at the Maha Kumbh in Haridwar, the most ra­pa­cious strain wins. Masking and so­cial dis­tanc­ing change the virus’s in­cen­tives, and it be­comes milder.

~ Amit Varma, glad they had dis­cussed se­man­tics, re­minded lis­ten­ers that all of this is metaphor. Past pan­demics, he noted, cit­ing Chinmay Tumbe’s *The Age of Pandemics*, ended not be­cause we elim­i­nated the strain but be­cause it evolved to­wards the least vir­u­lent. {125-R13}
stories.why: Public health does more than stop a dis­ease spread­ing, Shah’s story sug­gests. By mak­ing trans­mis­sion harder, clean water and masks change what a pathogen evolves into, and so can make the dis­ease it­self less deadly.
stories.postscript: Mid-explanation, Shah said of the pathogen, “Not that he’s think­ing.” Varma: “Not that he’s a he.” {125-J10}

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on cholera in the two Bengals

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on a mutation that built cattle cultures
stories.head: A mutation worth milking
body: All mam­mals make lac­tase as in­fants, to di­gest the lac­tose in milk, Ajay Shah said, and lose the abil­ity as they grow up.
Then, maybe 7,000 or 8,000 years ago, on the bor­der be­tween Bulgaria and Turkey, a mu­ta­tion let adults keep mak­ing it. {#lactase} The gene is called lac­tase per­sis­tence.

Milk be­came high-quality food for grown-ups, and whole cow-owning, cow-herding cul­tures grew around it. Its car­ri­ers re­pro­duced well and con­quered far­away lands, in­clud­ing north­ern India. The gene is still far more com­mon in India’s north, where those in­va­sions hap­pened, than in its south. {125-S08}
~ Not ev­ery­one wins. Amit Varma spared a thought for the lac­tose-intolerant, who lack the gene but live in a cul­ture that keeps ask­ing them why they don’t drink milk.

quote.text: there was a mu­ta­tion that was se­lected by nat­u­ral se­lec­tion and then the cul­ture turned around and ex­ploited that.

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on the gene for drinking milk

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on the deep-sea divers of Jeju Island
stories.head: Holding their breath for centuries
body: On Jeju Island in Korea, Ajay Shah said, women dive into the deep sea, for pearls as he put it, and div­ing has been the main liveli­hood for hun­dreds of years.

That set off nat­u­ral se­lec­tion. Women bet­ter able to hold their breath, process oxy­gen and cope with the pres­sure came back with the catch. Those less adapted tended to have ac­ci­dents and die. Over hun­dreds of years, the divers de­vel­oped re­mark­able phys­i­cal adap­ta­tions. {125-S09}
It is a bit like the Sherpas of the high Himalayas, Shah said, with their un­be­liev­able abil­ity to cope with low oxy­gen.
~ Amit Varma added that the world’s top long-distance run­ners come from East Africa, where al­ti­tude, ter­rain and cul­ture am­plify the ef­fect. {#runners}
stories.why: Natural se­lec­tion is not only an­cient his­tory, the story shows. A liveli­hood that presses on a pop­u­la­tion steadily, gen­er­a­tion after gen­er­a­tion, can vis­i­bly re­shape its bi­ol­ogy, as the sea did on Jeju.

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on the divers of Jeju Island

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on fogging, half-finished courses and resistance
stories.head: Half a dose, twice the trouble
body: When one hous­ing colony does DDT fog­ging, Ajay Shah said, the neigh­bour­ing build­ings get a par­tial dose. The mos­qui­toes that sur­vive are those with a lit­tle re­sis­tance, and they breed the next gen­er­a­tion. Do it at the scale of a pop­u­la­tion, he urged, not one colony at a time. {#fogging}

Antibiotics fail the same way. A full course drives a pathogen down so the im­mune sys­tem can fin­ish it off. But peo­ple start feel­ing bet­ter within two or three weeks and stop, leav­ing the most re­sis­tant pathogens to surge back. {#course}
Each im­per­fect cycle breeds an­timi­cro­bial re­sis­tance. The in­di­vid­ual feels fine, Shah said, “but at the level of a so­ci­ety, one by one we lose our sil­ver bul­lets.” {125-S11}
~ Amit Varma summed it up: “Evolutionary the­ory meets human hubris.” {#hubris}
stories.why: A par­tial dose is worse than none, be­cause it se­lects for re­sis­tance. Individual in­cen­tives, to fog one colony or stop a course on feel­ing bet­ter, wear down as­sets that be­long to ev­ery­one, which is why Shah calls this a pub­lic health prob­lem.

quiz.q: Why do sickle cell anaemia and thalassaemia persist, though they can fell someone running hard?
quiz.a: They are se­lected for where malaria is com­mon, mak­ing the plasmodium’s sur­vival harder.

quiz.q: Asked by a reporter how to get another Kapil Dev, what did the cricketer reply?
quiz.a: That his fa­ther was dead and his mother was too old.

quiz.q: What did Ajay Shah’s father teach his children using Dara Singh’s strong daughter?
quiz.a: That strength came from genes and up­bring­ing, not Dara Singh’s body­build­ing: not Lamarckism.

quiz.q: In Ajay Shah’s pencil ladder, what does the person on level two conclude?
quiz.a: That any­thing so com­plex needs a cen­tral com­mit­tee di­rect­ing the alu­minium and steel.

quiz.q: What, in Ajay Shah’s view, is the unit of evolutionary timescale?
quiz.a: Not time but gen­er­a­tions: hu­mans man­age about 400 in 10,000 years.

quiz.q: What happened to Britain’s white moths when industrial soot blackened the buildings?
quiz.a: Birds picked them off, and within a cou­ple of decades the moths turned black.

p4.credits: Everything is Everything was Amit Varma and Ajay Shah’s weekly show, 128 episodes from June 2023 to December 2025. This edition is made from Episode 125. The moving pictures, stills and chapter cards are from its video; the chapter art is by Simahina. Every play button starts the video at the moment it was said. The articles and headlines were written by Claude, an AI model, from the episode’s machine-made transcript, and checked against it. Other photographs are from Wikimedia Commons: Charles Darwin (Herbert Rose Barraud, public domain); Isaac Newton (Godfrey Kneller, public domain); David Hume (Allan Ramsay, public domain); Steven Pinker (Christopher Michel, CC BY-SA 4.0); Daniel Dennett (Dmitry Rozhkov, CC BY-SA 3.0). The covers on the shelf are from Amazon.

shelf.title: The Evolution of Everything
shelf.creator: Matt Ridley
shelf.why: Ridley finds the same bot­tom-up process, with no plan­ner or de­signer, be­hind nat­u­ral se­lec­tion, lan­guage, prices, cul­tural norms and com­mon law.

shelf.title: The Evolution of Everything (Episode 96 of The Seen and the Unseen, with Matt Ridley)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Amit’s long con­ver­sa­tion with Matt Ridley, a com­pan­ion to his book, on how order emerges bot­tom-up with­out cen­tral de­sign, across bi­ol­ogy, cul­ture and mar­kets.

shelf.title: I, Pencil
shelf.creator: Leonard Read
shelf.why: A pen­cil nar­rates its own mak­ing from ma­te­ri­als and know-how scat­tered across many coun­tries, co­or­di­nated by prices with no one in charge.

shelf.title: The Blank Slate
shelf.creator: Steven Pinker
shelf.why: Amit’s gate­way into nat­u­ral se­lec­tion and evo­lu­tion­ary psy­chol­ogy: Pinker ex­am­ines human na­ture and so­ci­ety through our evo­lu­tion­ary hard­wiring.

shelf.title: The Selfish Gene
shelf.creator: Richard Dawkins
shelf.why: Dawkins’s metaphor of the self­ish gene which, read care­fully rather than lit­er­ally, ex­plains why hu­mans are ca­pa­ble of love and al­tru­ism.

shelf.title: The Blind Watchmaker
shelf.creator: Richard Dawkins
shelf.why: Dawkins shows how in­tri­cate de­sign, like the eye, arises with­out a de­signer: the bi­o­log­i­cal coun­ter­part of Hayek’s point about economies.

shelf.title: Darwin’s Dangerous Idea
shelf.creator: Daniel Dennett
shelf.why: One of the core books the hosts learned evo­lu­tion from, by the thinker who framed it as an idea that dis­solves sim­ple pre­con­cep­tions.

shelf.title: The Moral Animal
shelf.creator: Robert Wright
shelf.why: Amit’s pick among books on nat­u­ral se­lec­tion be­cause it deals with moral­ity: how evo­lu­tion pro­duced our bet­ter in­stincts (it taught him ‘re­cip­ro­cal altruism’) and how mar­riage evolved, with monogamy and polygamy as adap­ta­tions to dif­fer­ent cir­cum­stances.

shelf.title: The Evolution of Human Sexuality
shelf.creator: Donald Symons
shelf.why: Symons used nat­u­ral se­lec­tion to ex­plain why men and women are wired dif­fer­ently: a for­ma­tive book for Amit that set off a flood of later work, its ar­gu­ments later con­firmed with data by A Billion Wicked Thoughts.

shelf.title: The Evolution of Cooperation
shelf.creator: Robert Axelrod
shelf.why: Axelrod uses game the­ory to show why we evolved to co­op­er­ate, and for­malises the best re­sponse to being wronged: strike back once, but not for­ever, so some pun­ish­ment is op­ti­mal but grudges are not.

shelf.title: A Billion Wicked Thoughts
shelf.creator: Ogi Ogas and Sai Gaddam
shelf.why: Uses hard data on anonymised in­ter­net be­hav­iour, re­vealed rather than stated pref­er­ences, to show what men and women want, and ex­plains why through nat­u­ral se­lec­tion.

shelf.title: The Age of Pandemics
shelf.creator: Chinmay Tumbe
shelf.why: Chinmay Tumbe’s his­tory of pan­demics: how cholera’s link to water was found and then re­sisted for decades, es­pe­cially in India, and how past pan­demics ended as strains evolved to­wards less vir­u­lent forms, which is why Amit ex­pected COVID to be­come some­thing we live with.

shelf.title: India’s Tryst With Pandemics (Episode 205 of The Seen and the Unseen, with Chinmay Tumbe)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: The deeper con­ver­sa­tion on the his­tory of pan­demics and how they play out.

shelf.title: Life Lessons
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Amit and Ajay’s course on what they wish they had been taught at twenty: learn­ing how to learn, frame­works for think­ing, writ­ing, prob­a­bilis­tic in­tu­ition, eco­nom­ics, the his­tory of thought, per­sonal fi­nance (Ajay’s mod­ule is ‘legendary’) and health.

laughs.text: Amit’s cold open: ‘Just a few mo­ments ago, Mr. Ajay Shah was telling me about a young fe­male mos­quito which got knocked up and came look­ing for mam­malian pro­teins, but un­for­tu­nately col­lided with my jeans pants. So noth­ing much is hap­pen­ing there.’
After Ajay re­cites F = GMm/r² and builds his pen­cil anal­ogy, Amit asks: ‘How many equa­tions do you know by heart, by the way?’
Amit il­lus­trat­ing the anger knob: your life could be nasty, brutish and hard, and ‘you keep meet­ing Bengali econ­o­mists and you can’t help shout­ing at them.’
On the spring­bok, whose showy leaps for mates let the lion wait for it to land, Amit: ‘I guess evo­lu­tion among the spring­boks could then be called a race to the top.’
On sickle cell’s trade-off be­tween out­run­ning a leop­ard and sur­viv­ing malaria, Amit: ‘I have a title for the short story. The Lion and the Mosquito.’ Ajay cor­rects: ‘The Lion or the Mosquito.’
Amit’s clos­ing pun after Ajay’s ode to the human and eagle eye: ‘The only kind of eye I don’t like, Ajay, is the I in ego.’

Douglas Adams, quoted by Amit on nat­u­ral se­lec­tion: ‘The awe it in­spired in me made the awe that peo­ple talk about in re­spect of re­li­gious ex­pe­ri­ence seem, frankly, silly be­side it. I take the awe of un­der­stand­ing over the awe of ig­no­rance any day.’

Eugenics wasn’t only Hitler’s project: Amit notes that H.G. Wells and George Bernard Shaw, both Fabian so­cial­ists and both in­spi­ra­tions for Nehru, also be­lieved in it. He sees it as the nat­u­ral­is­tic fal­lacy com­bined with Adam Smith’s ‘man of system’.
Ogi Ogas and Sai Gaddam on cul­ture shap­ing taste: ‘We can learn to ap­pre­ci­ate food that is bit­ter, like cof­fee or olives, but no cul­ture en­joys cin­na­mon sprin­kled feces.’
